flashcards.question: What is an accounting cycle?
flashcards.answer: The accounting cycle is the sequence of accounting procedures used to record, process, and report financial transactions during an accounting period, from initial transaction to preparation of financial statements and closing entries.

flashcards.question: What is cash basis accounting?
flashcards.answer: Cash basis accounting records revenues and expenses when cash is received or paid, regardless of when the transaction actually occurred.
flashcards.explanation: Simple method based on cash flow.

flashcards.question: What is accrual basis accounting?
flashcards.answer: Accrual basis accounting records revenues when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash is received or paid.
flashcards.explanation: GAAP requires accrual basis for most businesses.

flashcards.question: What is the posting procedure for special journals?
flashcards.answer: In special journals, individual transactions are not posted separately. Instead, column totals are posted periodically to the general ledger, reducing the number of postings required.

flashcards.question: What is a working trial balance?
flashcards.answer:
A working trial balance is an internal document that lists all account balances before adjustments.

Purpose:
• Verify debits equal credits
• Provide basis for adjusting entries
• Help prepare financial statements

flashcards.question: What is the purpose of adjusting entries?
flashcards.answer: Adjusting entries ensure that revenues and expenses are recognized in the correct accounting period under accrual accounting.

flashcards.question: What is the purpose of correcting entries?
flashcards.answer: Correcting entries are used to fix errors made in previously recorded transactions.

flashcards.question: What are typical adjustment areas for hospitality businesses at month end?
flashcards.answer:
Typical adjustments include:
• Accrued payroll
• Inventory adjustments
• Prepaid expenses
• Depreciation
• Unearned revenues
• Accrued expenses

flashcards.question: Why adjust Cost of Food Sales after storeroom issues are recorded?
flashcards.answer: Because storeroom issues represent actual usage, adjustments ensure that Cost of Food Sales reflects the true cost of food consumed, not just purchased.
flashcards.explanation: Match actual consumption to the period.

flashcards.question: Why does a business have unpaid payroll on payday?
flashcards.answer: Because employees earn wages up to the end of the pay period, but payment may occur later, creating accrued payroll expense that has not yet been paid.
flashcards.explanation: Timing difference between earning and paying.

flashcards.question: What does the computerized year-end process accomplish?
flashcards.answer:
The year-end process:
• Automatically posts closing entries
• Resets temporary accounts to zero
• Transfers net income/loss to retained earnings
flashcards.explanation: Prepares accounts for the new year.

flashcards.question: What does the post-closing trial balance signify?
flashcards.answer:
Post-closing trial balance confirms:
• Only permanent accounts remain open
• Debits equal credits
• The ledger is ready for the next accounting period

flashcards.question: What are the 10 steps of the Accounting Cycle?
flashcards.answer:
1. Analyze transactions
2. Journalize in general/special journals
3. Post to ledger
4. Prepare working trial balance
5. Journalize adjusting entries
6. Post adjusting entries
7. Prepare adjusted trial balance
8. Prepare financial statements
9. Journalize & post closing entries
10. Prepare post-closing trial balance
flashcards.explanation: Complete cycle from transaction to closing.

flashcards.question: What are the four types of Adjusting Entries?
flashcards.answer:
1. Prepaid Expenses (Deferrals) - paid now, expense later
2. Unearned Revenue (Deferrals) - received now, earn later
3. Accrued Expenses - incurred but not yet paid
4. Accrued Revenue - earned but not yet received

+ Depreciation adjustments
flashcards.explanation: Deferrals and accruals are key categories.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between Temporary and Permanent accounts?
flashcards.answer:
TEMPORARY (Nominal):
• Revenue, Expenses, Dividends
• Closed to zero at year end
• Start fresh each period

PERMANENT (Real):
• Assets, Liabilities, Equity
• NOT closed
• Balances carry forward
flashcards.explanation: Temporary accounts reset; permanent accounts continue.

flashcards.question: What are the four types of Special Journals?
flashcards.answer:
1. Sales Journal - credit sales only
2. Purchases Journal - credit purchases only
3. Cash Receipts Journal - all cash coming in
4. Cash Disbursements Journal - all cash going out

General Journal - for everything else

flashcards.question: What is the Matching Principle?
flashcards.answer:
The Matching Principle requires that expenses be recognized in the same period as the revenues they helped generate.

Example: If you sell products in January, the cost of those products should be expensed in January, not when purchased or paid.

flashcards.question: What is the Revenue Recognition Principle?
flashcards.answer:
Revenue should be recognized when:
1. It is earned (goods delivered or services performed)
2. It is realizable (payment is expected)

NOT when cash is received (that's cash basis, not GAAP).
flashcards.explanation: Recognize revenue when earned, not when paid.

learn.title: Accounting Cycle and Adjustments
learn.content:
📚 Chapter Overview: The Accounting Cycle

🔄 The Accounting Cycle = 10 Steps

From transactions → to financial statements → to closing

The accounting cycle is the complete sequence of procedures used to record, process, and report financial transactions during an accounting period.

📊 Two Accounting Methods

Cash Basis Accounting:
• Record revenue when CASH IS RECEIVED
• Record expense when CASH IS PAID
• Simple but not GAAP compliant
• Used by small businesses, individuals

Accrual Basis Accounting:
• Record revenue when EARNED
• Record expense when INCURRED
• Required by GAAP
• Used by most businesses

📝 Example: Cash vs Accrual

Hotel provides room service on Dec 31, guest pays on Jan 5:

Cash Basis: Record revenue in January (when paid)

Accrual Basis: Record revenue in December (when earned)

🔄 The 10 Steps of the Accounting Cycle

Step 1: Analyze business transactions

Step 2: Journalize transactions in journals

Step 3: Post to the general ledger

Step 4: Prepare working trial balance

Step 5: Journalize adjusting entries

Step 6: Post adjusting entries to ledger

Step 7: Prepare adjusted trial balance

Step 8: Prepare financial statements

Step 9: Journalize and post closing entries

Step 10: Prepare post-closing trial balance

📒 Types of Journals

Special Journals (for efficiency):
  • Sales Journal: Credit sales only
  • Purchases Journal: Credit purchases only
  • Cash Receipts Journal: All cash received
  • Cash Disbursements Journal: All cash paid out
General Journal:

For all transactions that don't fit in special journals (adjusting entries, correcting entries, unusual transactions).

Advantage of Special Journals: Column totals are posted periodically instead of posting each transaction separately - saves time!

📝 Types of Entries

1. Adjusting Entries

Ensure revenues and expenses are recognized in the correct period (accrual basis).

4 Types of Adjusting Entries:

DEFERRALS (paid/received now, recognize later):
• Prepaid Expenses - paid now, expense later
  Example: Prepaid insurance, prepaid rent

• Unearned Revenue - received now, earn later
  Example: Advance deposits, gift cards

ACCRUALS (recognize now, pay/receive later):
• Accrued Expenses - incurred but not yet paid
  Example: Wages payable, utilities payable

• Accrued Revenue - earned but not yet received
  Example: Interest receivable

📝 Adjusting Entry Example: Prepaid Insurance

Hotel paid $12,000 for 12 months insurance on Jan 1:

Monthly adjustment (expense $1,000):

Dr. Insurance Expense     $1,000
   Cr. Prepaid Insurance     $1,000

2. Correcting Entries

Fix errors in previously recorded transactions.

3. Closing Entries

Reset temporary accounts to zero at year end.

📊 Temporary vs Permanent Accounts

Temporary (Nominal) Permanent (Real)
Revenue accounts Asset accounts
Expense accounts Liability accounts
Dividends Equity accounts
CLOSED at year end NOT CLOSED - carry forward

🔒 The Closing Process

Closing Entries (in order):

1. Close Revenue accounts to Income Summary
Dr. Revenue     Cr. Income Summary

2. Close Expense accounts to Income Summary
Dr. Income Summary     Cr. Expenses

3. Close Income Summary to Retained Earnings
(Net income or loss transferred)

4. Close Dividends to Retained Earnings
Dr. Retained Earnings     Cr. Dividends

⚖️ Key Accounting Principles

Revenue Recognition Principle:

Recognize revenue when earned AND realizable (not when cash received).

Matching Principle:

Recognize expenses in the same period as the revenues they helped generate.

🏨 Hospitality-Specific Adjustments

  • Accrued Payroll: Employees earn wages but payday is later
  • Food Inventory: Adjust Cost of Food Sales for actual usage
  • Depreciation: Allocate cost of FF&E over useful life
  • Prepaid Expenses: Insurance, licenses, contracts
  • Unearned Revenue: Advance deposits, gift cards

✅ Trial Balances

Working Trial Balance:

Lists all account balances BEFORE adjustments. Verifies debits = credits.

Adjusted Trial Balance:

Lists all account balances AFTER adjusting entries.

Post-Closing Trial Balance:

Lists only PERMANENT accounts after closing. Confirms ledger is ready for new period.

Key Takeaways

  • Cash basis = record when cash moves; Accrual = record when earned/incurred
  • GAAP requires accrual basis accounting
  • 10 steps in the accounting cycle
  • Deferrals = paid/received now, recognize later
  • Accruals = recognize now, pay/receive later
  • Temporary accounts (Revenue, Expenses, Dividends) are CLOSED
  • Permanent accounts (Assets, Liabilities, Equity) carry forward

flashcards.question: What is the USAR?
flashcards.answer: The Uniform System of Accounts for Restaurants — a standardized chart of accounts and reporting format so restaurants of all sizes can record and compare results consistently.
flashcards.explanation: The restaurant equivalent of USALI for hotels.

flashcards.question: What are 'covers' in restaurant accounting?
flashcards.answer: Covers are the number of guests served (meals sold) during a period. They drive most restaurant performance ratios.

flashcards.question: How is average check calculated?
flashcards.answer: Average Check = Total Sales ÷ Number of Covers. It shows the average amount each guest spends.
flashcards.explanation: Total revenue spread over guests served.

flashcards.question: Compute average check: total food sales $513,000, covers 34,200.
What is seat turnover?
flashcards.answer: Seat Turnover = Covers ÷ Available Seats (for a period). It measures how many times each seat is used — i.e., how efficiently seating capacity is used.
flashcards.explanation: Higher turnover = seats reused more often.

flashcards.question: Compute seat turnover: 34,200 covers, 60 seats, 300 days.
What is food cost percentage?
flashcards.answer: Food Cost % = Cost of Food Sold ÷ Food Sales. It is the key cost-control ratio in a restaurant.
flashcards.explanation: Lower is better, within quality limits.

flashcards.question: What is beverage cost percentage?
flashcards.answer: Beverage Cost % = Cost of Beverage Sold ÷ Beverage Sales. Tracked separately from food because margins differ.
flashcards.explanation: Beverages usually have lower cost % than food.

flashcards.question: What is labor cost percentage?
flashcards.answer: Labor Cost % = Total Labor Cost ÷ Total Sales. A major controllable cost in restaurants.

flashcards.question: What is prime cost in a restaurant?
flashcards.answer: Prime Cost = Cost of Sales (food + beverage) + Total Labor Cost. It captures the two largest controllable costs combined.
flashcards.explanation: Often targeted at roughly 60–65% of sales.

flashcards.question: Why are food and beverage revenues reported separately?
flashcards.answer: Because they have different cost structures and margins; separating them lets managers control food and beverage cost percentages independently.

flashcards.question: What is the contribution margin of a menu item?
flashcards.answer: Contribution Margin = Selling Price − Variable (food) Cost. It is the amount each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs and profit.

learn.title: Restaurant Accounting & Analysis
learn.content:
🍽️ Chapter 9: Restaurant Accounting

Restaurants use the Uniform System of Accounts for Restaurants (USAR) so results can be recorded and compared consistently. Performance is driven by a handful of operating ratios.

📊 Key Operating Ratios

Average Check = Total Sales ÷ Covers
Seat Turnover = Covers ÷ Available Seats
Food Cost % = Cost of Food Sold ÷ Food Sales
Beverage Cost % = Cost of Beverage Sold ÷ Beverage Sales
Labor Cost % = Total Labor Cost ÷ Total Sales
Prime Cost = Cost of Sales + Labor Cost

Covers = guests served. Food and beverage revenues are tracked separately because their margins differ.

📝 Worked Example

Food sales $513,000, covers 34,200, seats 60, days open 300:

• Average Check = 513,000 ÷ 34,200 = $15.00
• Seat Turnover = 34,200 ÷ (60 × 300) = 1.9 times/day

🧮 Cost Control

Prime cost (cost of sales + labor) captures the two largest controllable costs and is the number managers watch most closely. Contribution margin (selling price − variable food cost) drives menu-engineering decisions.

Key Takeaways

  • USAR standardizes restaurant reporting.
  • Average check = sales ÷ covers; seat turnover = covers ÷ seats.
  • Food/beverage/labor cost % each = cost ÷ relevant sales.
  • Prime cost = cost of sales + labor cost.
  • Contribution margin = price − variable cost (menu engineering).

flashcards.question: What are the components of labor cost in the hotel industry?
flashcards.answer:
Labor cost includes:
• Wages and salaries
• Employee benefits
• Payroll taxes
• Service charge distributions
• Employee meals and uniforms

flashcards.question: What is the external statement showing revenues and expenses given to shareholders?
flashcards.answer: The Income Statement (also called Profit and Loss Statement or P&L).

flashcards.question: What revenue sources might be in Other Operated Departments?
flashcards.answer:
Revenue sources include:
• Spa operations
• Golf courses
• Parking
• Laundry/dry cleaning
• Health clubs
• Retail shops
• Recreational facilities

flashcards.question: What revenue sources might be in Rentals and Other Income?
flashcards.answer:
This includes:
• Space rentals
• Commission income
• Vending machine income
• Lease income
• Miscellaneous non-operating revenues

flashcards.question: What types of personnel might be in the A&G department?
flashcards.answer:
Administrative and General (A&G) includes:
• General management
• Accounting staff
• Human resources
• Information systems
• Clerical personnel

flashcards.question: What is a direct expense?
flashcards.answer: A direct expense is an expense that can be specifically identified with and charged to a particular department.

flashcards.question: What types of personnel might be in Sales and Marketing?
flashcards.answer:
Personnel include:
• Sales managers
• Marketing managers
• Advertising staff
• Public relations staff
• Reservation sales personnel

flashcards.question: Which department gets charged for repairs to Rooms department furniture?
flashcards.answer: The Rooms department will be charged for repairs to its furniture.

flashcards.question: What is the internal income statement given to managers called?
flashcards.answer: The Statement of Income and Expense (also called Departmental Income Statement).

flashcards.question: What four expenses are excluded from the internal income statement?
flashcards.answer:
Four excluded expenses:
1. Depreciation
2. Interest
3. Income taxes
4. Rent or lease expense (or replacement reserve)
flashcards.explanation: These are handled at corporate level.

flashcards.question: Which departments are Undistributed Operating Expenses?
flashcards.answer:
Undistributed Operating Expenses include:
• Administrative and General
• Sales and Marketing
• Property Operations and Maintenance
• Utilities
flashcards.explanation: Expenses not directly tied to revenue departments.

flashcards.question: What is Replacement Reserves on the internal statement?
flashcards.answer: Replacement Reserves represent funds set aside for future replacement of furniture, fixtures, and equipment (FF&E).

flashcards.question: What ratio measures actual room sales against potential room sales?
flashcards.answer: The Occupancy Percentage.

flashcards.question: What is gaming revenue in a casino operation?
flashcards.answer: Gaming revenue is the net amount retained by the casino, calculated as total wagers minus winnings paid to players.

flashcards.question: When is Complimentary Allowances used in a casino?
flashcards.answer: It is used when complimentary goods or services (rooms, food, entertainment) are provided to players and must be recorded as a reduction of gaming revenue.

flashcards.question: What is USALI?
flashcards.answer:
USALI = Uniform System of Accounts for the Lodging Industry

A standardized accounting system for hotels that:
• Provides consistent format for financial reporting
• Allows benchmarking across properties
• Separates operated departments from undistributed expenses
• Industry standard since 1926
flashcards.explanation: The gold standard for hotel accounting.

flashcards.question: What is RevPAR and how is it calculated?
flashcards.answer:
RevPAR = Revenue Per Available Room

Two calculation methods:
1. RevPAR = Total Room Revenue ÷ Available Rooms
2. RevPAR = ADR × Occupancy %

Measures how well a hotel fills rooms at an optimal rate.
flashcards.explanation: Key performance indicator for rooms department.

flashcards.question: What is GOPPAR?
flashcards.answer:
GOPPAR = Gross Operating Profit Per Available Room

GOPPAR = GOP ÷ Available Rooms

Measures overall hotel profitability on a per-room basis. Better than RevPAR because it accounts for all revenues AND expenses.

flashcards.question: What is ADR (Average Daily Rate)?
flashcards.answer:
ADR = Total Room Revenue ÷ Rooms Sold

Measures the average price guests pay per room. Used with occupancy to calculate RevPAR.

Higher ADR = higher room rates

flashcards.question: What is the difference between Operated and Undistributed Departments?
flashcards.answer:
OPERATED DEPARTMENTS:
• Generate revenue directly
• Rooms, F&B, Spa, Golf, etc.
• Have their own P&L statement

UNDISTRIBUTED DEPARTMENTS:
• Support operations but don't generate direct revenue
• A&G, Sales & Marketing, Maintenance, Utilities
• Costs allocated across property

flashcards.question: What is GOP (Gross Operating Profit)?
flashcards.answer:
GOP = Total Revenue − Department Expenses − Undistributed Expenses

GOP represents profit from operations BEFORE:
• Management fees
• Fixed charges (rent, insurance, property tax)
• Interest and depreciation

Key measure of operational performance.

learn.title: Hotel Income Statements & Departments
learn.content:
📚 Chapter Overview: Hotel Income Statements

🏨 USALI - Uniform System of Accounts for Lodging

Industry standard since 1926 • Currently 11th Edition

This chapter covers the unique aspects of hotel financial reporting, including USALI, departmental accounting, and key performance indicators.

📋 USALI - Uniform System of Accounts for the Lodging Industry

The industry-standard accounting framework for hotels since 1926. Currently in its 11th edition.

Benefits of USALI:
  • Standardized format for financial reporting
  • Enables benchmarking across properties
  • Facilitates comparison with competitors
  • Provides consistent departmental structure

🏨 Hotel Department Structure

OPERATED DEPARTMENTS (Generate Revenue):
• Rooms
• Food & Beverage
• Other Operated Departments (Spa, Golf, Parking, etc.)
• Rentals and Other Income

UNDISTRIBUTED OPERATING EXPENSES (Support Functions):
• Administrative & General (A&G)
• Sales & Marketing
• Property Operations & Maintenance (POM)
• Utilities

📊 Two Types of Income Statements

External (Shareholders) Internal (Managers)
Income Statement Statement of Income and Expense
Summarized Detailed by department
Includes all expenses Excludes: Depreciation, Interest, Taxes, Rent
Four Expenses EXCLUDED from Internal Statement:
  1. Depreciation
  2. Interest expense
  3. Income taxes
  4. Rent/lease expense (or Replacement Reserves)

📈 Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)

📊 Hotel KPI Formula to Remember!

RevPAR = ADR × Occupancy %

Revenue Per Available Room = Average Daily Rate × Occupancy

ROOMS KPIs:

Occupancy % = Rooms Sold ÷ Rooms Available
How full is the hotel?

ADR (Average Daily Rate) = Room Revenue ÷ Rooms Sold
Average price per occupied room

RevPAR = Room Revenue ÷ Available Rooms
OR RevPAR = ADR × Occupancy %
Revenue per available room (combines rate and occupancy)

📝 Example: KPI Calculations

Hotel has 200 rooms, sold 150 rooms, room revenue $22,500:

Occupancy: 150 ÷ 200 = 75%

ADR: $22,500 ÷ 150 = $150

RevPAR: $22,500 ÷ 200 = $112.50

Or: $150 × 75% = $112.50 ✓

PROFITABILITY KPIs:

GOP (Gross Operating Profit) =
Total Revenue − Department Expenses − Undistributed Expenses

GOPPAR = GOP ÷ Available Rooms
Overall profitability per room

👥 Labor Cost Components

  • Wages and salaries
  • Employee benefits (health insurance, retirement)
  • Payroll taxes (FICA, unemployment)
  • Service charge distributions
  • Employee meals and uniforms

🏢 Department Details

Administrative & General (A&G):
  • General management
  • Accounting staff
  • Human resources
  • Information systems
  • Clerical personnel
Sales & Marketing:
  • Sales managers
  • Marketing managers
  • Advertising staff
  • Public relations
  • Reservations sales
Direct vs Indirect Expenses:

Direct: Can be traced to specific department (furniture repair → Rooms)

Indirect: Shared across departments (utilities, insurance)

🎰 Gaming Operations (Casinos)

Gaming Revenue = Total Wagers − Winnings Paid to Players

Complimentary Allowances:
Comps (free rooms, meals, entertainment) given to players
Recorded as reduction of gaming revenue

🔧 Other Key Terms

Replacement Reserves:

Funds set aside for future replacement of Furniture, Fixtures & Equipment (FF&E). Typically 3-5% of revenue.

Other Operated Departments:
  • Spa operations
  • Golf courses
  • Parking
  • Laundry/dry cleaning
  • Health clubs
  • Retail shops
Rentals and Other Income:
  • Space rentals
  • Commission income
  • Vending machine income
  • Lease income

Key Takeaways

  • USALI = Industry standard for hotel accounting
  • RevPAR = ADR × Occupancy (memorize!)
  • ADR = Room Revenue ÷ Rooms SOLD
  • Occupancy = Rooms SOLD ÷ Rooms AVAILABLE
  • GOP = Profit BEFORE depreciation, interest, taxes
  • Internal statement excludes: Depreciation, Interest, Taxes, Rent
  • Gaming Revenue = Wagers − Winnings Paid

flashcards.question: What is depreciation?
flashcards.answer: The systematic allocation of the cost of a long-lived TANGIBLE asset (building, equipment, furniture) over its useful life, matching the expense to the periods that benefit from the asset.
flashcards.explanation: Spreading a fixed asset's cost over time.

flashcards.question: What is salvage (residual) value?
flashcards.answer: The estimated amount expected to be recovered at the end of an asset's useful life. It is subtracted from cost to find the depreciable base.
flashcards.explanation: What the asset is worth when retired.

flashcards.question: What is the depreciable base?
flashcards.answer: Depreciable Base = Cost − Salvage Value. It is the total amount that will be depreciated over the asset's life.
flashcards.explanation: The portion of cost that gets expensed.

flashcards.question: What is book value (carrying value)?
flashcards.answer: Book Value = Cost − Accumulated Depreciation. It is the asset's net amount reported on the balance sheet.

flashcards.question: What is the straight-line depreciation formula?
flashcards.answer: Annual Depreciation = (Cost − Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life. The same amount is expensed each year.

flashcards.question: Compute straight-line depreciation: cost $50,000, salvage $5,000, life 9 years.
What is the units-of-production method?
flashcards.answer: Depreciation = ((Cost − Salvage) ÷ Total Estimated Units) × Units Produced this period. Expense varies with actual usage.
flashcards.explanation: Ties depreciation to output, not time.

flashcards.question: What is the double-declining-balance (DDB) method?
flashcards.answer: An accelerated method: Depreciation = 2 × Straight-Line Rate × Beginning Book Value. Salvage is ignored in the calculation, but the asset is not depreciated below salvage value.

flashcards.question: What is MACRS?
flashcards.answer: The Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System — the depreciation method required by U.S. tax law, using set recovery periods and rates (differs from GAAP depreciation).

flashcards.question: What is the difference between depreciation, amortization, and depletion?
flashcards.answer:
• Depreciation — tangible fixed assets (equipment, buildings).
• Amortization — intangible assets (franchises, patents, goodwill).
• Depletion — natural resources (mines, timber).

flashcards.question: Why is land not depreciated?
flashcards.answer: Land has an unlimited useful life — it does not wear out or get used up — so its cost is not allocated to expense.
flashcards.explanation: The one fixed asset that isn't depreciated.

flashcards.question: How does accumulated depreciation appear on the balance sheet?
flashcards.answer: As a contra-asset (credit balance) subtracted from the related property & equipment, reducing it to book value.

learn.title: Depreciation & Amortization
learn.content:
📉 Chapter 11: Depreciation & Amortization

Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-lived tangible asset across the periods that benefit from it (the matching principle).

🔑 Key Terms

Depreciable Base = Cost − Salvage Value
Book Value = Cost − Accumulated Depreciation

🧮 Methods

Straight-Line = (Cost − Salvage) ÷ Useful Life — equal each year.

Units of Production = ((Cost − Salvage) ÷ Total Units) × Units this period.

Double-Declining-Balance (DDB) = 2 × Straight-Line Rate × Beginning Book Value — accelerated; ignores salvage in the formula but never depreciates below it.

MACRS = required for U.S. tax (different from GAAP).

📝 Straight-Line Example

Cost $50,000, salvage $5,000, life 9 years → (50,000 − 5,000) ÷ 9 = $5,000 per year.

🗂️ Depreciation vs Amortization vs Depletion

  • Depreciation — tangible fixed assets (equipment, buildings).
  • Amortization — intangibles (franchises, patents, goodwill).
  • Depletion — natural resources (mines, timber).

Land is never depreciated — its useful life is unlimited.

Key Takeaways

  • Depreciable base = cost − salvage; book value = cost − accumulated depreciation.
  • Straight-line = (cost − salvage) ÷ life (equal each year).
  • DDB is accelerated; MACRS is for taxes.
  • Amortization = intangibles; depletion = natural resources.
  • Land is not depreciated.

learn.title: Financial Analysis & Ratios
learn.content:
📚 Chapter Overview: Financial Analysis

📊 Financial Analysis = Understanding the Numbers

Ratios • Trends • Comparisons • CPA Services

This chapter covers financial statement analysis techniques, key ratios, and the services CPAs provide.

📈 Types of Financial Analysis

HORIZONTAL ANALYSIS:
• Compares same item across different TIME PERIODS
• Identifies trends and changes
• Example: Revenue 2023 vs Revenue 2024
• Also called "Trend Analysis"

VERTICAL ANALYSIS:
• Compares each item to a BASE within SAME PERIOD
• Shows percentage composition
• Balance Sheet base = Total Assets
• Income Statement base = Total Revenue
• Also called "Common-Size Analysis"

📊 Categories of Financial Ratios

1. Liquidity Ratios (Short-term ability to pay)
Current Ratio = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities
General short-term debt coverage

Quick Ratio = (Cash + Receivables + Securities) ÷ Current Liabilities
Excludes inventory (more conservative)

Hospitality Current Ratio = Same as Quick Ratio
Hotels use this because inventory isn't significant
2. Solvency Ratios (Long-term ability to pay)
Debt-to-Equity Ratio = Total Liabilities ÷ Total Equity
How much debt vs owner investment

Debt Ratio = Total Liabilities ÷ Total Assets
What portion of assets is financed by debt

Times Interest Earned = EBIT ÷ Interest Expense
How easily can the company pay interest
3. Profitability Ratios
Profit Margin = Net Income ÷ Revenue
Profit per dollar of sales

Return on Assets (ROA) = Net Income ÷ Total Assets
How well assets generate profit

Return on Equity (ROE) = Net Income ÷ Shareholders' Equity
Return to owners

Earnings Per Share (EPS) = (Net Income − Preferred Dividends) ÷ Weighted Avg Common Shares
Earnings per share of common stock
4. Activity Ratios (Asset Efficiency)
Inventory Turnover = Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Average Inventory
How fast inventory sells

Receivables Turnover = Revenue ÷ Average Receivables
How fast customers pay

Asset Turnover = Revenue ÷ Total Assets
Revenue generated per dollar of assets

👔 CPA Services (Three Levels of Assurance)

Service Assurance Level Description
Compilation None Just formats statements, no testing
Review Limited Inquiries and analytical procedures
Audit Reasonable Full examination, testing, opinion issued

Important!

Only CPAs can perform AUDITS! This is a licensed, exclusive service.

📋 Five Types of Audit Opinions

1. Unqualified (Clean) ✅
• BEST opinion - no problems found
• Statements fairly presented per GAAP

2. Unqualified with Explanatory Paragraph
• Clean opinion with added explanation
• Going concern issues, consistency changes

3. Qualified
• Minor issues or scope limitations
• "Except for..." language

4. Adverse ❌
• WORST opinion - major GAAP violations
• Statements NOT fairly presented

5. Disclaimer
• Auditor cannot express opinion
• Insufficient evidence or severe scope limitations

🏨 Hospitality-Specific Ratio

📝 Hospitality Current Ratio

Hotels use this modified current ratio because inventory is minimal:

(Cash + Receivables + Marketable Securities) ÷ Current Liabilities

Same as Quick Ratio - excludes inventory and prepaid expenses.

👥 Who Uses Financial Ratios?

  • Owners/Investors: Evaluate investment performance
  • Creditors/Lenders: Assess ability to repay loans
  • Management: Monitor operations, make decisions
  • Potential Investors: Decide whether to invest
  • Financial Analysts: Provide recommendations

Key Takeaways

  • Horizontal = Across time; Vertical = Within same period
  • Liquidity = Short-term; Solvency = Long-term
  • Hospitality Current Ratio excludes inventory (same as Quick Ratio)
  • Only CPAs can perform audits
  • Unqualified = Clean opinion (best)
  • Adverse = Major GAAP violations (worst)
  • ROE = Net Income ÷ Equity (return to owners)

flashcards.question: What two types of annual reports does the SEC require?

flashcards.question: What kind of agency is the SEC and what is its primary mission?
flashcards.answer:
The SEC is a federal government regulatory agency.

• Protect investors
• Maintain fair and efficient markets

flashcards.question: What is the significance of October 1929?
flashcards.answer: October 1929 marks the stock market crash, which led to the Great Depression and exposed serious weaknesses in financial reporting and market regulation.
flashcards.explanation: This crash led to creation of the SEC.

flashcards.question: Why was the SEC created?
flashcards.answer:
The SEC was created to:
• Restore investor confidence
• Prevent fraud and market manipulation
• Regulate the securities markets

Following the 1929 stock market crash.

flashcards.question: What is the importance of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (SOX)?
flashcards.answer:
SOX was enacted to:
• Increase corporate accountability
• Improve financial reporting accuracy
• Strengthen internal controls

In response to corporate scandals like Enron and WorldCom.

flashcards.question: What do the key sections of Sarbanes-Oxley cover?
flashcards.answer:

Section 409: Real-time disclosure of material changes
Section 802: Criminal penalties for altering/destroying records
flashcards.explanation: Know these section numbers and their purposes.

flashcards.question: What is a 10-K report?
flashcards.answer:
A 10-K is a comprehensive annual filing to the SEC including:
• Audited financial statements
• Management discussion and analysis
• Risk factors
• Detailed disclosures about operations and finances

flashcards.question: What four types of audit opinions can a CPA firm give?
flashcards.answer:
1. Unqualified opinion (clean opinion)
2. Qualified opinion (with exceptions)
3. Adverse opinion (statements not fairly presented)
4. Disclaimer of opinion (unable to form opinion)
flashcards.explanation: Unqualified is the best; adverse is the worst.

flashcards.question: What are consolidated financial statements?
flashcards.answer: Consolidated financial statements combine the financial results of a parent company and its subsidiaries into a single set of statements as if they were one economic entity.

flashcards.question: What are notes to financial statements and what do they include?
flashcards.answer:
Notes provide additional information to understand financial statements.

Minimum content:
• Summary of significant accounting policies
• Detailed explanations of major accounts
• Information on contingencies and commitments
flashcards.explanation: Notes are essential for full disclosure.

flashcards.question: What is the standard content of an annual report to shareholders?
flashcards.answer:
Standard content includes:
• Letter from management
• Financial statements
• Notes to financial statements
• Auditor's report
• Management's Discussion and Analysis (MD&A)
flashcards.explanation: All key components of the annual report.

flashcards.question: What is the Securities Act of 1933?
flashcards.answer:
The Securities Act of 1933 (the 'Truth in Securities' Act) requires:
• Registration of new securities with SEC
• Full disclosure via prospectus
• Accurate information to investors before purchase

Focus: PRIMARY market (new issues)

flashcards.question: What is the Securities Exchange Act of 1934?
flashcards.answer:
The Securities Exchange Act of 1934:
• Created the SEC
• Regulates secondary trading of securities
• Requires ongoing periodic reporting (10-K, 10-Q)
• Regulates stock exchanges and broker-dealers

Focus: SECONDARY market (trading)

flashcards.question: What is PCAOB?
flashcards.answer:
PCAOB = Public Company Accounting Oversight Board

Created by SOX 2002 to:
• Oversee audits of public companies
• Establish auditing standards
• Inspect CPA firms
• Enforce compliance

Replaced self-regulation by accounting profession.

flashcards.question: What is Materiality in auditing?
flashcards.answer:
Materiality is the threshold above which an omission or misstatement would influence a user's decision.

Auditors focus on material items because:
• Not practical to examine everything
• Small errors unlikely to affect decisions
• Cost-benefit consideration
flashcards.explanation: Significant enough to matter to users.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between 10-K and 10-Q?
flashcards.answer:
10-K: Annual report
• Audited financial statements
• Filed within 60-90 days of fiscal year end
• Comprehensive disclosure

10-Q: Quarterly report
• Unaudited financial statements
• Filed within 40-45 days of quarter end
• Less detailed than 10-K

learn.title: SEC, Annual Reports & Audits
learn.content:
📚 Chapter Overview: SEC, Annual Reports & Audits

🏛️ SEC - Securities and Exchange Commission

Federal regulatory agency protecting investors since 1934

This chapter covers the regulatory framework for financial reporting, including the SEC, securities laws, Sarbanes-Oxley Act, and the audit process.

📜 Historical Background

⚠️ October 1929: The Stock Market Crash

The crash led to the Great Depression and exposed serious weaknesses in financial reporting and market regulation. Investors lost confidence due to fraud and manipulation.

Timeline of Securities Regulation:
  • 1929: Stock market crash
  • 1933: Securities Act (regulates NEW securities)
  • 1934: Securities Exchange Act (creates SEC, regulates TRADING)
  • 2002: Sarbanes-Oxley Act (response to Enron/WorldCom scandals)

🏛️ The SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission)

A federal government regulatory agency with three primary missions:

  1. Protect investors
  2. Maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets
  3. Facilitate capital formation

📋 Key Securities Laws

Securities Act of 1933 ("Truth in Securities")
• Regulates PRIMARY market (new securities offerings)
• Requires registration of new securities
• Requires prospectus with full disclosure
• Focus: BEFORE securities are sold
Securities Exchange Act of 1934
• Created the SEC
• Regulates SECONDARY market (trading)
• Requires ongoing periodic reporting (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K)
• Regulates stock exchanges and broker-dealers
• Focus: AFTER securities are sold

⚖️ Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (SOX)

⚠️ SOX 2002 - Response to Corporate Scandals

Enron • WorldCom • Tyco → Increased corporate accountability

Enacted in response to corporate scandals (Enron, WorldCom, Tyco) to increase corporate accountability and improve financial reporting.

Key SOX Sections - MEMORIZE THESE:

Section 302: Management Certification
CEO and CFO must personally certify financial statements are accurate

Section 401: Off-Balance-Sheet Disclosure
Must disclose all material off-balance-sheet transactions

Section 404: Internal Control Assessment ⭐
Management must assess and report on internal controls; auditors must attest

Section 409: Real-Time Disclosure
Material changes must be disclosed rapidly

Section 802: Criminal Penalties
Up to 20 years for altering/destroying records

Memory Tip!

302 = Certification (CEO/CFO sign off)

404 = Controls (like 404 error - something's broken!)

802 = Criminal (8 = handcuffs shape!)

PCAOB (Public Company Accounting Oversight Board)

Created by SOX to oversee audits of public companies:

  • Establishes auditing standards
  • Inspects CPA firms
  • Enforces compliance
  • Replaced self-regulation by accounting profession

📊 Annual Reports

Two Types Required by SEC:
Form 10-K Annual Report to Shareholders
Filed with SEC Given to shareholders
Detailed, technical Reader-friendly, summarized
Audited financial statements Audited financial statements
Extensive disclosures, risk factors Letter from CEO, highlights
Standard Content of Annual Report:
  • Letter from management
  • Financial statements
  • Notes to financial statements
  • Auditor's report
  • Management's Discussion and Analysis (MD&A)
Other SEC Filings:
  • 10-Q: Quarterly report (unaudited)
  • 8-K: Current report for material events
  • Proxy Statement: For shareholder meetings

🔍 The Audit Process

Four Types of Audit Opinions:
1. Unqualified Opinion (Clean Opinion) ✅
Best outcome - statements fairly presented in all material respects

2. Qualified Opinion ⚠️
Good EXCEPT for specific issue(s) - "except for" language

3. Adverse Opinion ❌
Statements are NOT fairly presented - material misstatements

4. Disclaimer of Opinion 🚫
Auditor cannot form an opinion - scope limitation
Audit vs Review vs Compilation:
Service Assurance Level Procedures
Audit Highest Detailed testing, confirmations, inspection
Review Limited Inquiry and analytical procedures
Compilation None Simply presents management's data
Materiality

Materiality is the threshold above which an omission or misstatement would influence a user's decision. Auditors focus on material items because it's not practical to examine everything.

Consolidated Financial Statements

Combine the financial results of a parent company and its subsidiaries into a single set of statements, as if they were one economic entity.

Key Takeaways

  • 1929 crash → 1933 & 1934 Acts → SEC created
  • SOX 2002: Response to Enron/WorldCom scandals
  • Section 302 = CEO/CFO certification
  • Section 404 = Internal controls (most tested!)
  • Section 802 = Criminal penalties
  • Unqualified = BEST audit opinion
  • Audit > Review > Compilation (assurance level)

flashcards.question: What is a budget?
flashcards.answer: A budget is a formal written financial plan that expresses management's expectations for revenues, expenses, and profits for a future period.
flashcards.explanation: Budgets guide business operations and planning.

flashcards.question: What are the advantages of budgeting?
flashcards.answer:
Budgeting advantages:
• Provides a plan for future operations
• Improves coordination and communication
• Helps control costs and expenses
• Serves as a standard for performance evaluation
• Encourages management discipline
flashcards.explanation: Budgeting is essential for business success.

flashcards.question: Why can predicting sales be difficult?
flashcards.answer:
Sales prediction is difficult due to uncertain factors:
• Economic conditions
• Competition
• Consumer behavior
• Seasonality
• Pricing changes
• Unexpected events

flashcards.question: What is sales forecasting?
flashcards.answer: Sales forecasting is the process of estimating future sales revenue for a given period. It forms the foundation for budgeting, staffing, purchasing, pricing, and profit planning.

flashcards.question: What factors should be considered in forecasting sales for a new business?
flashcards.answer:
Factors include:
• Market size and demand
• Location
• Target customers
• Competition
• Pricing strategy
• Management experience
• Economic conditions
• Marketing plans

flashcards.question: What is the formula for forecasting room sales?
flashcards.answer: Room Sales = Number of Available Rooms × Occupancy Percentage × Average Room Rate (ADR)
flashcards.explanation: Key formula for hotel revenue forecasting.

flashcards.question: What is the formula for forecasting food sales?
flashcards.answer: Food Sales = Number of Seats × Turnover × Average Check
flashcards.explanation: Key formula for restaurant revenue forecasting.

flashcards.question: What three kinds of expenses are closely related to sales?
flashcards.answer:
1. Food cost
2. Labor cost
3. Other variable operating expenses
flashcards.explanation: These expenses change with sales volume.

flashcards.question: What is the total cost equation?
flashcards.answer: Total Cost = Fixed Costs + Variable Costs

flashcards.question: What is a variable expense?
flashcards.answer: A variable expense changes directly in proportion to sales volume. Examples: food cost, beverage cost, commissions.

flashcards.question: What is a fixed expense?
flashcards.answer: A fixed expense remains constant regardless of sales volume within a relevant range. Examples: rent, insurance, management salaries.
flashcards.explanation: Fixed costs don't change with sales.

flashcards.question: What is a semi-variable expense?
flashcards.answer: A semi-variable expense contains both fixed and variable components. Example: utilities (base charge + usage).

flashcards.question: What is the difference between breakeven and breakeven point?
flashcards.answer:
Breakeven is the condition where total revenues equal total costs (zero profit/loss).

Breakeven point is the specific level of sales or volume at which breakeven occurs.

flashcards.question: What is the breakeven point formula?
flashcards.answer:
Breakeven Point (in sales) = Fixed Costs ÷ Contribution Margin Ratio

OR

Breakeven Point (in units) = Fixed Costs ÷ Contribution Margin per Unit

flashcards.question: What is Contribution Margin?
flashcards.answer:
Contribution Margin = Sales Revenue − Variable Costs

It's the amount that 'contributes' to covering fixed costs and generating profit.

CM Ratio = Contribution Margin ÷ Sales Revenue

flashcards.question: What is Margin of Safety?
flashcards.answer:
Margin of Safety = Actual Sales − Breakeven Sales

It measures how much sales can drop before the company reaches breakeven (starts losing money).

Margin of Safety % = (Actual Sales − Breakeven) ÷ Actual Sales
flashcards.explanation: Higher margin of safety = lower risk.

flashcards.question: What is Operating Leverage?
flashcards.answer:
Operating Leverage measures how sensitive operating income is to changes in sales.

Degree of Operating Leverage = Contribution Margin ÷ Operating Income

High operating leverage = high fixed costs = greater risk but greater reward
flashcards.explanation: High leverage amplifies both profits and losses.

flashcards.question: What is CVP Analysis?
flashcards.answer:
CVP (Cost-Volume-Profit) Analysis examines the relationship between:
• Costs (fixed and variable)
• Volume (sales quantity)
• Profit

Used for pricing, product mix, and break-even decisions.

flashcards.question: What is a Flexible Budget?
flashcards.answer:
A flexible budget adjusts for changes in activity level, showing expected costs at various volumes.

Unlike a static budget, it recognizes that costs change with sales volume.

Useful for performance evaluation - compare actual results to budgeted amounts at actual activity level.

flashcards.question: What is the High-Low Method?
flashcards.answer:
The High-Low Method separates fixed and variable costs using the highest and lowest activity levels:

Variable Cost per Unit = (High Cost − Low Cost) ÷ (High Activity − Low Activity)

Fixed Costs = Total Cost − (Variable Cost × Activity Level)
flashcards.explanation: Simple method to analyze mixed costs.

learn.title: Budgeting, Forecasting & Cost Analysis
learn.content:
📚 Chapter Overview: Budgeting & Cost Analysis

📊 CVP Analysis = Cost-Volume-Profit

Understanding the relationship between costs, sales volume, and profit

This chapter covers budgeting fundamentals, sales forecasting, cost behavior, and Cost-Volume-Profit (CVP) analysis - essential tools for hospitality management.

📋 What is a Budget?

A budget is a formal written financial plan that expresses management's expectations for revenues, expenses, and profits for a future period.

Advantages of Budgeting:
  • Provides a plan and direction for operations
  • Improves coordination between departments
  • Helps control costs and evaluate performance
  • Encourages efficient use of resources
  • Assists in decision-making

⚠️ Why Budgeting is Difficult:

Sales prediction is affected by uncertain factors: economic conditions, competition, consumer behavior, seasonality, pricing changes, and unexpected events.

🔮 Sales Forecasting

Sales forecasting is the process of estimating future sales revenue. It forms the foundation for all other budgeting activities.

Key Forecasting Formulas:

ROOM SALES:
Room Sales = Available Rooms × Occupancy % × ADR

FOOD SALES:
Food Sales = Seats × Turnover × Average Check

📝 Example: Hotel Room Sales Forecast

A hotel has 200 rooms, expects 75% occupancy, ADR of $150:

Daily Room Sales = 200 × 0.75 × $150 = $22,500

Monthly (30 days) = $22,500 × 30 = $675,000

📝 Example: Restaurant Sales Forecast

Restaurant has 100 seats, 2.5 turns per meal, $35 average check:

Sales per Meal Period = 100 × 2.5 × $35 = $8,750

💰 Cost Behavior

Understanding how costs behave is essential for budgeting and decision-making.

Total Cost Equation:
Total Cost = Fixed Costs + Variable Costs

Or: TC = FC + (VC per unit × Volume)
Types of Costs:
Type Behavior Examples
Variable Changes proportionally with sales Food cost, beverage cost, commissions
Fixed Stays constant regardless of sales Rent, insurance, management salaries
Semi-variable Has both fixed and variable components Utilities, telephone, maintenance
Three Expenses Closely Related to Sales:
  1. Food Cost - varies directly with food sales
  2. Labor Cost - varies with business volume
  3. Other Variable Operating Expenses

📊 CVP Analysis (Cost-Volume-Profit)

CVP analysis examines the relationship between costs, sales volume, and profit. It's used for pricing decisions, product mix, and break-even analysis.

Key CVP Formulas:

Contribution Margin (CM):
CM = Sales Revenue − Variable Costs

CM per Unit:
CM per Unit = Selling Price − Variable Cost per Unit

CM Ratio:
CM Ratio = CM ÷ Sales Revenue

📝 Example: Contribution Margin

Hotel room sells for $200, variable cost per room is $40:

CM per Unit = $200 − $40 = $160

CM Ratio = $160 ÷ $200 = 80%

This means 80 cents of every dollar contributes to covering fixed costs and profit!

⚖️ Breakeven Analysis

📈 Break-Even Point

Total Revenue = Total Costs

No profit, no loss - the starting point for profitability!

Breakeven is the condition where Total Revenue = Total Costs (zero profit/loss).

Breakeven Point is the specific sales level where breakeven occurs.

Breakeven Formulas:

In Sales Dollars:
BE Point = Fixed Costs ÷ CM Ratio

In Units:
BE Point = Fixed Costs ÷ CM per Unit

📝 Example: Breakeven Calculation

Hotel has Fixed Costs of $500,000, CM Ratio of 80%:

Breakeven = $500,000 ÷ 0.80 = $625,000 in sales

The hotel needs $625,000 in revenue just to cover all costs!

🛡️ Margin of Safety

Measures how much sales can drop before reaching breakeven.

Margin of Safety:
MOS = Actual Sales − Breakeven Sales

MOS % = (Actual Sales − Breakeven) ÷ Actual Sales

📝 Example: Margin of Safety

Actual Sales = $800,000, Breakeven = $625,000:

MOS = $800,000 − $625,000 = $175,000

MOS % = $175,000 ÷ $800,000 = 21.9%

Sales can drop 21.9% before the hotel starts losing money!

⚡ Operating Leverage

Measures how sensitive operating income is to changes in sales.

Degree of Operating Leverage:
DOL = Contribution Margin ÷ Operating Income

High Operating Leverage = High fixed costs = Greater risk BUT greater reward potential

Low Operating Leverage = High variable costs = Lower risk BUT lower profit potential

📈 The High-Low Method

A simple technique to separate mixed costs into fixed and variable components.

High-Low Method Steps:

Step 1: Variable Cost per Unit =
(Highest Cost − Lowest Cost) ÷ (Highest Activity − Lowest Activity)

Step 2: Fixed Costs =
Total Cost − (Variable Cost × Activity Level)

Key Takeaways

  • Room Sales = Rooms × Occupancy × ADR
  • Food Sales = Seats × Turnover × Avg Check
  • Total Cost = Fixed + Variable
  • Contribution Margin = Sales − Variable Costs
  • Breakeven = Fixed Costs ÷ CM Ratio
  • Margin of Safety = Actual − Breakeven
  • Higher leverage = higher risk AND higher potential reward

flashcards.question: What items are included in cash?
flashcards.answer:
Cash includes:
• Currency and coins on hand
• Bank deposits
• Checks received from customers
• Money orders
• Other negotiable instruments
• Undeposited cash receipts
• Cash in house banks
flashcards.explanation: Cash must be readily available for use.

flashcards.question: What is the definition of internal control?
flashcards.answer:
Internal control is a system of policies and procedures designed to:
• Protect assets
• Ensure accurate accounting records
• Promote operational efficiency
• Encourage adherence to management policies
flashcards.explanation: Internal control is the foundation of reliable financial reporting.

flashcards.question: What are the four main objectives of internal control?
flashcards.answer:
1. Safeguarding assets
2. Ensuring reliability and accuracy of accounting records
3. Promoting operational efficiency
4. Ensuring compliance with laws and company policies
flashcards.explanation: These objectives protect the business from fraud and errors.

flashcards.question: What assets are intended to be safeguarded by internal control?
flashcards.answer:
Assets to be safeguarded include:
• Cash
• Inventory
• Equipment
• Furnishings
• Supplies
• Other property
• Accounting records
• Financial information
flashcards.explanation: Both physical assets and information need protection.

flashcards.question: What is collusion?
flashcards.answer: Collusion occurs when two or more employees work together to circumvent internal control procedures, usually to commit fraud or theft that would be difficult for one person to accomplish alone.
flashcards.explanation: Collusion is a significant threat to internal controls.

flashcards.question: What is the advantage of bonding employees?
flashcards.answer:
Bonding employees:
• Provides financial protection against losses caused by employee dishonesty
• Acts as a deterrent to theft or fraud
• Allows recovery of losses by the company
flashcards.explanation: Bonded employees know that losses can be recovered.

flashcards.question: What is an internal control procedure for house banks?
flashcards.answer: Assign responsibility for each house bank to one specific employee and require that the bank be counted and reconciled at the beginning and end of each shift.

flashcards.question: What is the purpose of the cashier's daily report?
flashcards.answer:
The cashier's daily report:
• Summarizes all cash transactions for the day
• Reconciles cash received with recorded sales
• Provides documentation for accounting and management review
flashcards.explanation: Essential for cash control and accountability.

flashcards.question: What is the purpose of a bank reconciliation?
flashcards.answer:
Bank reconciliation:
• Explains differences between bank statement and company's cash records
• Detects errors or irregularities
• Ensures accuracy of the cash account
flashcards.explanation: Reconciliation is a key control procedure.

flashcards.question: What are canceled checks?
flashcards.answer: Canceled checks are checks that have been paid by the bank and returned to the check writer as proof of payment.
flashcards.explanation: They serve as evidence that payment was made.

flashcards.question: What is a deposit in transit?
flashcards.answer: A deposit in transit is cash receipts that have been recorded by the company but not yet recorded by the bank.

flashcards.question: What are outstanding checks?
flashcards.answer: Outstanding checks are checks that have been written and recorded by the company but not yet paid by the bank.
flashcards.explanation: Timing difference - bank hasn't processed yet.

flashcards.question: What is an NSF check?
flashcards.answer: NSF (Non-Sufficient Funds) check is a check returned by the bank because the issuer does not have enough funds in their account to cover the check.

flashcards.question: Why does the bank statement balance generally not equal the checkbook balance?
flashcards.answer:
Balances differ due to timing differences:
• Outstanding checks
• Deposits in transit
• Bank service charges
• NSF checks
• Errors by bank or company
flashcards.explanation: These items are recorded at different times.

flashcards.question: What are the 5 components of COSO Internal Control Framework?
flashcards.answer:
1. Control Environment - tone at the top, ethics, integrity
2. Risk Assessment - identifying and analyzing risks
3. Control Activities - policies and procedures
4. Information & Communication - relevant info flows
5. Monitoring Activities - ongoing evaluations
flashcards.explanation: COSO framework is the gold standard for internal control.

flashcards.question: What is Separation of Duties and why is it important?
flashcards.answer:
Separation of Duties means dividing responsibilities among different employees so no single person controls all aspects of a transaction.

Three functions to separate:
• Authorization
• Custody of assets
• Record keeping

This prevents fraud and errors.
flashcards.explanation: One person should never handle a transaction from start to finish.

flashcards.question: What is a Petty Cash Fund?
flashcards.answer:
A petty cash fund is a small amount of cash kept on hand to pay for minor expenses that are impractical to pay by check.

Controls include:
• Fixed fund amount
• One custodian responsible
• Receipts required for all disbursements
• Periodic surprise counts

flashcards.question: What are prenumbered documents and why are they used?
flashcards.answer:
Prenumbered documents are forms (checks, invoices, receipts) printed with sequential numbers.

Purpose:
• Track all documents
• Detect missing or duplicate transactions
• Establish audit trail
• Prevent unauthorized transactions
flashcards.explanation: Essential for transaction tracking and accountability.

flashcards.question: What is the purpose of surprise audits?
flashcards.answer:
Surprise audits are unannounced examinations of records or cash.

Benefits:
• Deter fraud (employees don't know when audit will occur)
• Detect irregularities before they grow
• Test effectiveness of controls
• Keep employees vigilant
flashcards.explanation: The element of surprise is key to effectiveness.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between authorization and approval?
flashcards.answer:
Authorization: General permission to perform transactions within set limits (e.g., manager can approve purchases up to $500)

Approval: Specific permission for a particular transaction (e.g., signing a specific purchase order)

Both are control activities that ensure proper review.
flashcards.explanation: Authorization sets limits; approval is for specific actions.

flashcards.question: What are the steps in a Bank Reconciliation?
flashcards.answer:
1. Start with bank statement ending balance
2. Add: Deposits in transit
3. Subtract: Outstanding checks
4. = Adjusted bank balance

5. Start with book balance
6. Add: Bank collections, interest earned
7. Subtract: Service charges, NSF checks
8. = Adjusted book balance

Both adjusted balances should match!
flashcards.explanation: Systematic process to reconcile two balances.

flashcards.question: What is a Cash Over and Short account?
flashcards.answer:
Cash Over and Short is an account used to record differences between actual cash and the amount that should be in the cash register.

• Debit (expense) if cash is SHORT
• Credit (revenue) if cash is OVER

Large or frequent differences indicate control problems.
flashcards.explanation: Tracks cashier accuracy and potential theft.

learn.title: Cash and Internal Control
learn.content:
📚 Chapter Overview: Cash and Internal Control

This chapter covers the fundamentals of cash management and the internal control systems that protect a hospitality business's most liquid asset.

💰 What is Cash?

In accounting, cash refers to the most liquid assets that are readily available for use. Cash includes:

  • Currency and coins on hand
  • Bank deposits (checking and savings accounts)
  • Checks received from customers
  • Money orders and traveler's checks
  • Other negotiable instruments
  • Undeposited cash receipts
  • Cash in house banks (front desk, restaurants, bars)

⚠️ NOT Cash:

Accounts receivable, inventory, prepaid expenses, and investments are NOT considered cash because they cannot be immediately used for payments.

🛡️ Internal Control Definition

Internal control is a comprehensive system of policies, procedures, and practices designed by management to:

4 Main Objectives of Internal Control:

1. Safeguard Assets - Protect cash, inventory, equipment from theft or misuse

2. Ensure Accuracy - Maintain reliable and accurate accounting records

3. Promote Efficiency - Encourage operational effectiveness

4. Ensure Compliance - Adhere to laws, regulations, and company policies

🏛️ COSO Internal Control Framework

🏗️ COSO = Committee of Sponsoring Organizations

The Gold Standard for Internal Control - 5 Interrelated Components

The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations (COSO) framework is the gold standard for internal control. It has 5 interrelated components:

5 Components of COSO Framework:

1. Control Environment
The "tone at the top" - management's integrity, ethical values, and commitment to competence

2. Risk Assessment
Identifying and analyzing risks that may prevent achieving objectives

3. Control Activities
Policies and procedures that ensure management directives are carried out (approvals, authorizations, verifications, reconciliations)

4. Information & Communication
Relevant information must be identified, captured, and communicated in a timely manner

5. Monitoring Activities
Ongoing evaluations to assess whether controls are functioning effectively

🔐 Key Control Principles

Separation of Duties

The most critical internal control principle. No single person should control all aspects of a transaction. Three functions must be separated:

  • Authorization - Approving transactions
  • Custody - Physical control of assets
  • Record Keeping - Recording transactions

📝 Example: Hotel Front Desk

• Night auditor (records) ≠ Cashier (custody) ≠ Manager (authorization)

• If one person does all three, they could steal cash and cover it up in records!

Prenumbered Documents

All important documents (checks, invoices, receipts) should have sequential numbers to:

  • Track all transactions
  • Detect missing or duplicate documents
  • Establish an audit trail
Bonding Employees

Fidelity bonds provide insurance against employee dishonesty. Benefits:

  • Financial recovery if theft occurs
  • Deterrent effect - employees know losses can be recovered
  • Background checks during bonding process
Surprise Audits

Unannounced examinations of cash and records. The unpredictability is the key - employees never know when an audit might occur.

🏨 House Banks in Hospitality

A house bank is a fixed amount of cash assigned to a cashier for making change. Controls include:

  • One specific employee responsible for each bank
  • Count and reconcile at beginning and end of each shift
  • Bank amount should remain constant
  • Overages and shortages investigated
Petty Cash Fund

A small amount of cash kept for minor expenses. Controls:

  • Fixed fund amount (e.g., $200)
  • One custodian responsible
  • Receipts required for ALL disbursements
  • Cash + Receipts must always equal fund total

🏦 Bank Reconciliation

📊 Bank Statement ↔️ Company Records

Reconciliation ensures both balances match after adjustments

A bank reconciliation explains differences between the bank statement balance and the company's book balance. It should be performed monthly by someone who does NOT handle cash.

Bank Reconciliation Procedure:

BANK SIDE:
Bank Statement Balance
+ Deposits in Transit
− Outstanding Checks
± Bank Errors
= Adjusted Bank Balance

BOOK SIDE:
Book Balance (per records)
+ Bank Collections, Interest Earned
− Service Charges, NSF Checks
± Book Errors
= Adjusted Book Balance

Both adjusted balances must be equal!
Key Terms:
  • Deposit in Transit: Recorded by company but not yet by bank (ADD to bank)
  • Outstanding Check: Written by company but not yet paid by bank (SUBTRACT from bank)
  • NSF Check: "Bounced" check - insufficient funds (SUBTRACT from books)
  • Canceled Check: Check that has been paid and returned as proof

📊 Cash Over and Short

When actual cash differs from expected amount:

  • Cash Short: Actual < Expected → Debit (expense)
  • Cash Over: Actual > Expected → Credit (revenue)

Large or frequent differences indicate control problems and should be investigated!

🚨 Collusion

Collusion occurs when two or more employees work together to circumvent internal controls. It's the biggest threat to any control system because:

  • Separation of duties is defeated
  • Harder to detect than individual fraud
  • Usually involves larger amounts

Key Takeaways

  • Internal control protects assets and ensures accurate records
  • COSO framework has 5 components - memorize them!
  • Separation of duties = Authorization + Custody + Record keeping SEPARATED
  • Bank reconciliation reconciles BANK balance with BOOK balance
  • Deposits in transit: ADD to bank; Outstanding checks: SUBTRACT from bank
  • Collusion defeats separation of duties
